title: Indulgences, honestly (CCC 1471–1479)
hook: not buying forgiveness; a release from lingering effects of sin through the Church's prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, many forms of penance: fasting, prayer, almsgiving, and a long list of everyday turns. Your line was many ways back. Which one did you choose? Day one thousand one hundred three.

A baseball goes through a neighbor's window. The kid knocks on the door, red in the face, and says sorry. The neighbor says, I forgive you. And she means it. The friendship is fine. But the window is still broken, and the glass is still on the floor. Forgiveness happened. Repair hasn't yet. Hold on to that window, because today's word has a reputation, and some of what people have heard about it is wrong. Today we take it slowly and honestly.
screen: `A BALL THROUGH THE WINDOW.` → `FORGIVEN.` → `STILL BROKEN GLASS.`

segments.voice: First, what an indulgence is not. It is not forgiveness of sin. The Catechism is clear that an indulgence only touches sins whose guilt has already been forgiven. The apology and the pardon come first, in confession. So what is left? Catholic teaching says sin has two kinds of consequence. One is the break with God, which forgiveness heals. The other it calls temporal punishment: the leftover damage, the bent habits, the attachments that still pull, the glass on the floor. That damage needs healing, here or, Catholics believe, in purgatory. An indulgence, the Catechism says, is a release from some or all of that leftover punishment, through the Church. Partial, or plenary, which means full. Second, where it comes from. Not from the person's own effort alone. The Catechism points to the communion of saints, the belief that all of God's people, living and dead, are bound together, so that the holiness of one helps the others. It calls this the Church's treasury: the merits of Christ, and the prayers and good works of Mary and the saints. The Church opens that treasury on the person's behalf, attaching it to a prayer, a pilgrimage, a work of mercy, done with a turned heart. And Catholics can offer an indulgence for someone who has died. Third, the part that has to be said honestly. There were times when indulgences were preached for money, and that abuse became one of the sparks of the Reformation. Martin Luther's protest began there, and Christians still read that history differently. Catholic teaching today is plain on the point that matters most: forgiveness was never something a person could buy. An indulgence, done rightly, asks for a changed heart, not a payment. That's today's line.
screen: `NOT FORGIVENESS: THE GUILT IS ALREADY GONE.` · `THE LEFTOVER DAMAGE OF SIN.` · `THE COMMUNION OF SAINTS, A TREASURY.` · `ONCE SOLD. NEVER FOR SALE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn the difference. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been forgiven for, by a friend, a parent, a partner, or, if you pray, by God. The forgiveness is real. Now notice what's still on the floor. A habit that keeps pulling. Trust that's still mending. A sharpness you still reach for. Don't scold yourself. Just name one piece of glass. If you pray, you can ask for help with that repair. If you don't, simply notice that being forgiven and being healed can be two different moments. The bell holds the time.

Indulgence. In Catholic teaching, a release, through the Church's prayer and the communion of saints, from the lingering effects of sins already forgiven. Not forgiveness itself, and not for sale. Today's word.
Your line: never for sale. Today, when you hear someone say indulgence, or use it yourself, remember the window: forgiven first, repaired after. Day one thousand one hundred three.

howItsDone: Catholics may seek an indulgence by doing a prayer or work the Church names, such as a pilgrimage or a work of mercy, together with confession, Communion and prayer for the pope's intentions, and they may offer it for someone who has died.

what it means: a release from the leftover effects of sins already forgiven, never forgiveness itself, and never for sale.

notes: Catechism paraphrased throughout (copyrighted translation); no direct quotations.
The broken-window image is a common catechetical analogy for guilt versus temporal punishment, not the Catechism's own; Keeper may prefer another.

History: 'indulgences were preached for money, and that abuse became one of the sparks of the Reformation. Martin Luther's protest began there.' Not stated in CCC 1471–1479; kept without dates or names of preachers under the claims rule. Confirm the phrasing is fair to Lutheran and Catholic readers alike.

'Catholic teaching today is plain ... forgiveness was never something a person could buy': confirm. The Council of Trent's and later reforms' rulings on the sale of indulgences are deliberately not cited.

howItsDone names the usual conditions for a plenary indulgence (confession, Communion, prayer for the pope's intentions); confirm the wording, and that 'pilgrimage or a work of mercy' are fair examples.
